title: Agency Positioning Maturity Score
subtitle: Measures how clearly your agency is built around a distinct position, the right clients, and pricing that reflects the value you actually deliver.

questions.text: When a prospective client asks who you work with, how do you respond?

answers.label: I describe a broad range — we work with any business that needs marketing help.
I name an industry or two, but the description still fits a lot of agencies.
I can name a specific client type, though I sometimes hedge depending on who's asking.
I name a specific client profile — revenue stage, situation, and what they're trying to solve.
I can say it in one sentence, it's been tested on real conversations, and prospects recognize themselves in it.

questions.text: How much of your current messaging came from analyzing competitors?

answers.label: Most of it — we tracked what others were doing and wrote ours to be competitive.
A fair amount — we used competitor research as a starting point.
Some, but we made a point of adding our own perspective.
Very little — we looked outward briefly, then focused on what was true about our own work.
None — we built positioning entirely from our client files and actual outcomes.

questions.text: How does your messaging hold up when a prospect compares you to three similar agencies?

answers.label: It covers similar ground — we rely on relationship or price to differentiate.
We have a few points of difference, but they could describe other agencies too.
We have a distinct angle, though we haven't tested it in direct comparisons.
Our messaging is specific enough that prospects say we sound different from others they've talked to.
We consistently hear that we were the only agency that spoke to their actual situation.

low.headline: Your positioning is borrowed, not built.
low.text: The work that creates distinct positioning starts inside your own client files, not in competitor decks. When you build messaging from the outside in, you end up replicating what already exists — and your message drifts toward everyone else's without you noticing it.
steps: Pull your last 10 to 15 client engagements and identify the 3 to 4 where you did your best work. What did those clients have in common?
Write down the specific revenue stage, problem, and desired outcome for each of those clients. Look for the pattern.
Draft a positioning sentence: '[We work with] [specific client type] [at this stage] [trying to accomplish this specific outcome].' Test it on a real conversation before you polish the website.

mid.headline: You have directional clarity — now get specific.
mid.text: You're past the generic stage, but there's still hedging in how you talk about who you serve. The agencies that win the comparison conversation are specific enough that prospects feel like the message was written for their exact situation.
steps: Go back to your positioning statement and cut the language that could apply to more than one kind of client.
Identify the revenue stage and the specific trigger moment when your best clients typically come to you — and put both in writing.
Test the specificity: can a prospect read your positioning and know within 10 seconds whether they're the right fit?

high.headline: Your positioning is doing the work it should.
high.text: You've built messaging from the inside out — from real client outcomes, not competitor templates. That clarity is what makes new business conversations easier and client alignment stronger.
steps: Document the positioning logic so it travels with your team — not just in your head.
Review it every six months against your most recent client files to make sure it still reflects who you do your best work with.
Use it as the filter for every new business conversation: if the prospect doesn't match, that's information.

questions.text: How are your current clients distributed across the revenue stages you serve?

answers.label: We take whoever comes — there's no consistent pattern in who we work with.
Most clients are in a similar range, but we haven't made deliberate choices about it.
We have a target client profile, though we still take work outside it when needed.
The majority of our client base fits the profile we've defined as the right fit.
We turn away work that doesn't fit the profile, and our roster reflects that discipline.

questions.text: How did your messaging change the last time you raised your rates or repositioned?

answers.label: We raised rates but didn't change the messaging — we hoped clients wouldn't notice the difference.
We updated pricing but the repositioning was mostly cosmetic.
We updated messaging and pricing at the same time, though we weren't sure they were aligned.
We rebuilt the offer and the messaging together, then tested both before going to market.
The repositioning was driven by client outcome data — we knew exactly what changed and why it justified the shift.

questions.text: How many active client retainers are you running right now?
questions.hint: Count only ongoing retainer relationships, not one-off projects.

questions.text: What is your average monthly retainer value across those clients?
questions.hint: Use your actual average, not your target rate.

low.headline: You're building revenue without building a client base.
low.text: Taking whoever comes feels like filling pipeline — but it's actually diluting your positioning every time you say yes to work that doesn't fit. The agencies that scale past $3M without destroying margins have usually made deliberate choices about who they serve long before they needed to.
steps: Define the exact client profile that produced your best engagements — revenue stage, business type, and the problem they came to you with.
Calculate what percentage of your current roster actually fits that profile. That number tells you how much correction you need.
For your next three new business conversations, practice turning down the work that doesn't fit before it becomes a client relationship.

mid.headline: You have a client base forming — now make it intentional.
mid.text: You're moving in the right direction, but there's likely some drift in who you're working with. The clients that feel hardest to serve are usually the ones that didn't fit the profile when you brought them on.
steps: Review your current roster and flag the clients that are misaligned — different revenue stage, different problem set, different expectations.
Build a plan to transition those relationships or reframe the engagement rather than absorbing the misfit.
Use your best current clients as the template for every new business conversation.

high.headline: Your client selection is working as a growth lever.
high.text: Disciplined client selection is one of the highest-leverage things an agency owner can do — and most skip it because saying no feels expensive in the short term. You're past that.
steps: Document the criteria you use when you turn down work — make it explicit so your team can apply the same filter.
Review your average retainer value annually against the effort each client requires. That ratio tells you whether your pricing has kept pace with your selectivity.
Use your best clients as case studies that attract more of the same.

questions.text: How did you set the price on your most recent new client engagement?

answers.label: We based it on what we thought the client would accept.
We looked at what comparable agencies charge and priced near that range.
We estimated hours, applied a rate, and added a margin.
We priced based on the outcome the client was trying to achieve and what that was worth to them.
We had a structured conversation about the client's financial situation, defined the outcome, and built the price from there — before any scope was discussed.

questions.text: How has AI changed your pricing or offer structure in the past 12 months?

answers.label: It hasn't — we're still using the same model we had before AI tools were available.
We've adopted AI tools but haven't changed how we price the work.
We've had internal conversations about it, but haven't made changes yet.
We've adjusted at least one offer or pricing tier to account for what AI has changed in how we produce the work.
We've rebuilt how we talk about and price deliverables to reflect the value we create rather than the time we spend.

questions.text: When AI reduces the hours required to produce a deliverable, what happens to your price?

answers.label: The price drops — we price by hours, so fewer hours means a lower invoice.
We haven't worked this out yet — it varies by engagement.
We try to hold the price, but clients sometimes push back on hours-based billing.
We've mostly moved away from hourly pricing so efficiency gains stay with the agency.
Our pricing is fully tied to outcomes — AI making us faster increases our margin, not our invoice, and clients know that's how it works.

questions.text: How many hours per week does your team spend on research, brief-writing, and competitive context — before any creative or production work begins?
questions.hint: Include all senior and mid-level hours spent at the thinking and synthesis stage, not production.

low.headline: Your pricing model is eroding your margins as AI changes the work.
low.text: The agencies that are figuring out AI pricing are decoupling price from time. The agencies still guessing are watching their per-hour math fall apart as production gets faster. The split was clear enough that I built a presentation around it at a room of 250 agency owners.
steps: Identify your three highest-volume deliverables and calculate what percentage of the price is justified by hours versus the outcome it creates for the client.
For any deliverable where AI has cut production time by 30% or more, rewrite the offer description to lead with the outcome, not the process.
Pick one offer to reprice on an outcome basis and test it on your next three new business conversations before rolling it out.

mid.headline: You're aware of the shift — now build the structure to capture it.
mid.text: Knowing that pricing needs to change and building the structure to change it are two different things. The agencies that get this right don't just raise prices — they rebuild how they talk about what they sell so the price makes sense before the conversation turns to numbers.
steps: For each major offer, write a one-paragraph description that leads with the client outcome and makes no mention of hours or deliverable volume.
Build a pricing logic document that your team can use in new business conversations — not a rate card, but a framework for how you arrive at a number.
Test your new framing on existing clients before you roll it out to new business.

high.headline: Your pricing reflects the value you create, not the time you spend.
high.text: You've made the structural shift that most agencies are still avoiding. Outcome-based pricing is harder to sell initially and far more durable once it's established — and it's the only model that actually benefits from AI getting faster.
steps: Document the pricing logic in enough detail that a new team member could walk a prospect through it.
Review your price points annually against your actual margin per engagement — efficiency gains should be showing up there.
Use your pricing structure as a filter: clients who only want to buy hours aren't the right fit for how you work.

categories.name: Senior Hours & Where Thinking Actually Happens

questions.text: Where do your most senior people spend most of their time each week?

answers.label: Mostly in production — reviewing, editing, and reformatting work before it goes out.
Split between production oversight and client communication, with little time for upstream thinking.
Primarily in client-facing work, though the upstream brief and strategy work still gets compressed.
Mostly in strategy, brief development, and the thinking that shapes what gets produced.
Almost entirely in the judgment calls — brief quality, client situation, strategic direction — with production handled below them.

questions.text: How are you using AI tools right now in your agency workflow?

answers.label: Primarily for content production — generating drafts, captions, and copy at volume.
For production tasks and some client reporting automation.
For production and some research tasks, though the brief and strategy work is still done manually.
We use AI to accelerate research and competitive context before the brief, which changes what the brief looks like.
AI shapes the inputs before the thinking starts — brief quality is different because the research arrives faster and more completely.

questions.text: When a campaign underperforms, what does the diagnosis usually reveal?

answers.label: The execution was off — production errors, timing issues, or platform problems.
The content volume wasn't high enough — we needed more posts or more ads.
The creative wasn't strong enough, but the brief was solid.
The brief had gaps — research was thin and the insight wasn't sharp enough.
We trace it back to the brief every time, which is why we protect the upstream thinking hours.

low.headline: Your senior hours are being spent in the wrong place.
low.text: The hours where thinking actually shapes what gets made are the brief, the research, and the competitive context. When those hours get compressed or skipped, production volume doesn't fix it — five posts that nobody engages with aren't better than one post that drives results, and the tool doesn't change that math.
steps: Map out where your most senior person spent their last 10 working days. Calculate the percentage in upstream thinking versus production oversight.
Identify which production tasks could move down or be assisted by AI, freeing senior hours for brief and strategy work.
Set a minimum floor for brief development time per engagement — and protect it even when the timeline is tight.

mid.headline: You're protecting some of the right hours — now protect more of them.
mid.text: The brief and the research are where the thinking shapes the work. AI adoption concentrates at the production end at most agencies — the hours that stay manual are the ones that actually determine performance.
steps: Pilot AI-assisted research and competitive context for your next three briefs. Measure whether brief quality changes when inputs arrive faster.
Remove one senior production oversight task and redirect those hours to upstream brief development.
Track campaign performance against brief quality scores over the next quarter — the correlation is usually visible within eight weeks.

high.headline: Your senior hours are doing the work that actually determines performance.
high.text: You've made the structural choice that most agencies avoid: protecting the thinking hours even when production pressure is high. That's where the quality difference actually lives.
steps: Build a brief quality standard that your team can evaluate before work enters production.
Use AI to accelerate research inputs further — if the brief is already better, faster inputs make it better still.
Document the brief development process so it scales as you grow without losing what makes it work.

questions.text: What does your growth plan look like for the next 12 months?

answers.label: We don't have a formal plan — we take opportunities as they come.
We have a revenue target but no clear plan for how we'll get there.
We have a target and some ideas, but the path isn't fully mapped.
We have a target, a clear client acquisition strategy, and defined offer tiers.
We have a target, a client profile, an offer structure, a pricing logic, and a plan for how each feeds the next — and we review it quarterly.

questions.text: How do you know whether your agency is on track to hit its next revenue milestone?

answers.label: We check the bank account and see how the month went.
We track revenue but not the leading indicators that drive it.
We track revenue and a few activity metrics, but they're not tightly connected.
We track pipeline, close rate, average retainer value, and churn — and we know what to adjust when they move.
We have a financial model that connects every growth lever to the revenue outcome, and we use it to make decisions rather than react to results.

low.headline: You're running the agency reactively.
low.text: The move from $150K to $1M and from $3M to $10M look very different — but both require the same thing: a clear map of how each part of the business connects to the outcome you're building toward. Without that, growth is mostly luck managed at close range.
steps: Write down your revenue target for 12 months from now. Then work backward: how many clients, at what average retainer, with what close rate, do you need to get there?
Identify the two or three numbers that, if they changed, would most directly move your revenue — and start tracking those weekly.
Build or update a simple financial model that shows you the relationship between new business activity and revenue outcomes. A spreadsheet is enough.

mid.headline: You have some of the structure — close the gaps.
mid.text: You're tracking some of the right things, but there are likely gaps between what you measure and the decisions you make. The agencies that build past their current milestone without losing margins are usually running a tighter feedback loop between their numbers and their choices.
steps: Identify the one leading indicator you're not tracking that would give you the most useful signal — usually pipeline coverage or average deal size.
Set a cadence for reviewing your key metrics — weekly for pipeline, monthly for margin, quarterly for positioning fit.
Connect your financial model to your offer structure so you can see what a rate increase or a new service tier actually does to your trajectory.

high.headline: You're running the business, not just the agency.
high.text: The difference between an agency and a business is whether the owner has a model for how decisions connect to outcomes. You're past the stage where growth is a reaction to what shows up — you're making it happen.
steps: Formalize your financial model so it can travel with a leadership team member, not just you.
Build a review rhythm that catches drift early — positioning, pricing, client mix, and margins deserve a quarterly look.
Use your model to stress-test the next growth move before you make it — new hire, new service line, new market.

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: In 30 minutes I'll show you which two gaps to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing.
